homonyms.basis: The census row carries no disambiguation field. No card is a homonym: all eight cards concern the workshop. The name 'Wordcraft' alone, the census's alias, redirects on Wikipedia to Rhetoric (B10, F87), a homonym in the common noun. Wordcraft, the tool, is a distinct object from the workshop that used it (B8 F51; ActuIA cites its own paper, 'Wordcraft: a Human-AI Collaborative Editor for Story Writing', arXiv:2107.07430, 15 Jul 2021, B3); the searches for the cards' URLs also returned unrelated namesakes (the WordCraft Writers' Forum of Literature Wales; Wordcrafters, a nonprofit in Eugene, Oregon; a Gemini API sample app named Wordcraft on ai.google.dev), recorded here as distinct entities and not admitted to the field.
distinct_entities: Wordcraft, the tool: the LaMDA-powered editor built by Google PAIR (B8 F51; its paper arXiv:2107.07430, cited in B3)
the whitepaper, Creative Writing with an AI-Powered Writing Assistant: Perspectives from Professional Writers (B9; arXiv:2211.05030)
the thirteen stories, each its writer's work (B1 F5)
the WordCraft Writers' Forum (Literature Wales), Wordcrafters (Eugene, Oregon), a Gemini API sample app named Wordcraft (search results, not admitted)

captures.description: THE WORKSHOP, SIGNED OUT, 2026-11-01: 'The Wordcraft Writers Workshop was a 2022 research project by Google’s PAIR (People + AI Research) and Magenta teams that explored AI-augmented creative writing.' Overview and setup (the tool, its features, the cohort 'under non-disclosure agreements', the results); '2026 Literary Backlash' (the project 'resurfaced widely on social media (such as Bluesky)' in August 2026; the criticism that participants 'had lent credibility to AI models trained on copyrighted literary works without consent'; participants' responses). Eight cards: Google (two), Magenta, ActuIA, The Algorithmic Bridge, Engadget, Coralflavor, Mezha.

atoms.evidence: The Wordcraft Writers Workshop was a 2022 research project
by Google’s PAIR (People + AI Research) and Magenta teams
Participants used Wordcraft, an experimental text editor powered by Google’s LaMDA language model.
Thirteen diverse professional authors (including Ken Liu, Robin Sloan, and Eugenia Triantafyllou) spent eight weeks writing short stories with the tool
